stops.name: Kherson and the Crimea, Potemkin's roads
stops.campa: Landing at Kherson as winter closes the steppe, Miranda is taken up by Prince Potemkin himself, who carries the American through the newly conquered Crimea: Perekop, Bakhchisarai with its fountains, the new fleet a-building at Sevastopol. The Prince of Taurida shows off his half-built empire; his guest, connoisseur of empires, misses nothing. Potemkin, delighted, writes ahead to the Empress: there travels with him a Spanish American of extraordinary parts. The road to Kiev is being paved with Potemkin's letters.

stops.name: Kiev: Catherine the Great
stops.campa: On 14 February 1787, in Kiev where the court has paused on the imperial progress to the Crimea, Miranda is presented to Catherine the Great. The Empress questions the American about his warm country while the Dnieper lies frozen outside; she keeps him beside her for weeks, at cards, at table, in the long conversations the courtiers learn to envy. Her favor becomes his shield: protection in her embassies, and the right to wear the Russian uniform in every court of Europe, an empress's cloth over the fugitive's shoulders. Spain's ambassadors will claw at it in vain.
stops.quote: Las bondades que Vuestra Majestad Imperial se ha dignado dispensarme desde mi presentación en Kiev han penetrado de tal modo mi alma, que quedaré inviolablemente ligado a su Augusta Persona.
stops.quote_source: Carta de Miranda a Catalina II, 1787 (Colombeia)

stops.name: St. Petersburg, the Empress's protection
stops.campa: In St. Petersburg the favor ripens into instruments: letters commanding Russia's ambassadors to receive and protect Colonel Miranda wherever he presents himself, a purse for the road, the uniform confirmed. The Spanish envoy protests; Catherine's ministers shrug with imperial politeness. Miranda studies the Hermitage, the corps of cadets, the machinery of enlightened autocracy: the most absolute throne in Europe sheltering the man who will spend the rest of his life pulling thrones down. When he drives out of Petersburg in September, he travels as Russia's guest and Spain's nightmare.

stops.name: Stockholm, the courts of the North
stops.campa: Through Finland to Stockholm, where Gustav III's theatrical court receives the Russian-uniformed American; then the long Scandinavian winter: Norway's mines, Denmark's prisons. In Copenhagen he inspects the dungeons and is appalled, and intercedes with the ministers for wretches he will never see again; years later, in chains himself, the canon will remember the symmetry. He examines schools, canals, dockyards, constitutions. The ledger of Europe is nearly complete: he has now weighed every kind of king, and found the balance owing to republics.

stops.name: London, the return; the Plan begins
stops.campa: On 18 June 1789, with France three weeks from its Bastille, Miranda re-enters London through the Low Countries and Switzerland, the grand tour closed: four years, every court from Potsdam to Petersburg, the ruins of Athens and the maneuvers of kings, all reduced to notes and conclusions. The conclusion is single: Spanish America must be free, and England can be made to help. He unpacks the sixty trunks of his education and begins drafting the great Plan. The traveller is finished; the Precursor begins.

stops.name: Hollwood, Kent: Pitt and the great Plan
stops.campa: On 14 February 1790, at Hollwood, William Pitt receives Miranda in secret. The Nootka Sound quarrel has England arming against Spain, and the American lays the whole design on the minister's table: the emancipation of Spanish America, its geography, its revenues, its future constitution, an empire of liberty from the Mississippi to Cape Horn, offered to Britain's interest. Pitt listens, takes the papers, and files the continent for later use. It is the Plan's first audience with power. Spain and England make peace; Miranda and patience begin their long war.

stops.name: Paris, the Revolution calls
stops.campa: In the spring of 1792 Miranda crosses to Paris, where the Revolution is arming against the kings of Europe. Pétion and the Girondins embrace the famous American; here is a man who has studied war on three continents and liberty on two. Within months the Republic makes him maréchal de camp: the highest military rank any American has yet held in Europe. He accepts on his own terms: France's fight is the rehearsal, Spanish America the performance. The Girondins promise him, when the tide turns, an army for the Indies.

stops.name: The Argonne, the defiles held
stops.campa: September 1792: Brunswick's Prussians pour toward Paris and Dumouriez throws his ragged army across the forest passes of the Argonne: the Thermopylae of France, he calls them. Miranda commands in the defiles, holds his ground when Croix-aux-Bois is lost, and covers the army's regrouping. The canon counts these wooded ridges among the places where the Revolution was saved before it was won. The American general, veteran of Melilla, Algiers and Pensacola, now stands between the old monarchies and the first republic of Europe.

stops.name: Valmy, the cannonade
stops.campa: On 20 September 1792, at the mill of Valmy, the artillery of France stands against the army of the kings and does not break. Miranda commands in the line of the victorious cannonade: the battle after which Goethe, watching from the Prussian side, declares that a new era of world history has begun. A son of Caracas is a general of that new era on its first day. For this campaign his name will be carved on the Arc de Triomphe: MIRANDA, the only American on the arch, the stone the canon reads as prophecy.

stops.name: Antwerp, the command in Belgium
stops.campa: After Jemappes the Republic's armies flood into Belgium, and Miranda directs the siege of Antwerp: the citadel capitulates at the end of November 1792 and the general of Caracas enters the city on the Scheldt as its liberator. He governs with the moderation he preaches, property respected, priests unhanged, and dreams on paper of carrying the war to Spain itself and thence to America. He stands now at the height of the French service: commander of the Army of the North in Dumouriez's absence, one victory from everything.

stops.name: Neerwinden, the defeat and the accusation
stops.campa: At Neerwinden, 18 March 1793, the Austrians break the French left, Miranda's wing, and the Republic loses Belgium in an afternoon. Dumouriez, already bargaining his own treason with the enemy, needs a foreigner to wear the blame, and denounces his American lieutenant to Paris even as he himself prepares to defect. The pattern the canon marks: the Precursor's disasters are always another man's treachery, and the accusers always desert to the enemy while the accused rides to face the tribunal. Miranda goes to Paris to answer: voluntarily, head high, into the Terror.

stops.name: Paris, the Revolutionary Tribunal; acquittal
stops.campa: Before the Revolutionary Tribunal, the machine that acquits almost no one, Miranda defends himself for four days with the coolness of a man reading from his own archive. Witnesses, documents, the geometry of the battle: he takes the court through Neerwinden like a staff lecture. On 16 May 1793 the jury acquits him and the crowd carries the American general from the courtroom on its shoulders through the streets of Paris. Danton's turn will come; Miranda walks out. The canon counts it among his victories: he defeated the Terror in its own temple.
